questions.question: In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. Agent $i$ is not allowed to do task $j$. How is this forbidden pair represented in the cost matrix used for row and column reductions?
options: By deleting row $i$ and column $j$ from the cost matrix
By the entry 0, so that the pair is removed from the costs
By a large finite entry that the first reduction turns into 0
By the entry $\infty$, kept infinite through all reductions

questions.question: In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. One pair has $c_{ij}=\infty$ because it is forbidden, and at least one complete assignment avoids every forbidden pair. Can an optimal assignment use the pair $(i,j)$?
options: Yes, if the other entries in its assignment are cheap enough.
No, an assignment through it has infinite cost, above any allowed one.
Yes, but only when no other assignment has a finite total cost.
Yes, when its row and column contain only large finite costs.

questions.question: The assignment problem $\min\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$ with $\sum_jx_{ij}=1$ for each agent $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=1$ for each task $j$ and $x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$ must forbid agent 2 from doing task 3. Which added constraint does this?

In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. In one instance, agent 2 is forbidden from every task, so every entry of row 2 is $\infty$. What can be concluded?
options: Agent 2 is given a dummy task at zero cost and the rest is solved.
Agent 2 takes the task with the smallest cost in its column.
No complete assignment can avoid every forbidden pair in this instance.
The other agents are assigned first, and agent 2 takes the rest.

questions.question: In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. To forbid agent 1 from doing task 2, a student deletes row 1 and column 2 from the cost matrix and solves the smaller problem. What does this actually model?
options: The ban itself, since agent 1 can no longer reach task 2.
Agent 1 is fixed to task 2, the opposite of the ban.
Only the removal of agent 1; task 2 is still assigned.
The ban, but with the optimal cost lowered by $c_{12}$.

questions.question: Three machines (rows) must be assigned to three jobs (columns) one-to-one, with cost matrix entries $c_{ij}$ for machine $i$ on job $j$. Machine 2 cannot process job 3. Which change to the cost matrix models this?
options: Set every entry in column 3 of the matrix to $\infty$.
Set $c_{32}$ to $\infty$, reading the job as the row.
Give machine 2 an infinite cost for every one of the jobs.
Set $c_{23}$, the cost of machine 2 on job 3, to $\infty$.

questions.question: After row and column reductions, an assignment problem with forbidden pairs has reduced matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&\infty&0\\\infty&0&2\\0&1&\infty\end{pmatrix}$ (rows agents, columns tasks). Which complete assignment uses only zero entries?

Two agents and two tasks have costs $c_{11}=1$, $c_{21}=2$, $c_{22}=9$, and agent 1 is forbidden from task 2. A modeller enters the finite penalty $M=5$ for $c_{12}$ and picks the one-to-one assignment of least total cost. What does the model choose?
options: Agent 1 on task 2 and agent 2 on task 1, cost 7, via the banned pair
Agent 1 on task 1 and agent 2 on task 2, cost 10, respecting the ban
No assignment at all, since the penalty makes the problem infeasible
Agent 1 on task 1 and agent 2 on task 1, cost 3, the two row minima

questions.question: A $3\times3$ assignment problem (rows agents, columns tasks; each agent one task, each task one agent) forbids the pairs $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,1)$. Which complete assignment respects all bans?

In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. Forbidden pairs have entry $\infty$. Why must such an entry stay infinite when finite numbers are subtracted from rows and columns, rather than being replaced by some finite value?
options: Replacing it changes the number of complete assignments.
A finite stand-in makes the row minimum negative.
A finite stand-in can be reduced to 0 and then be selected.
Replacing it is harmless, as reductions never create zeros there.

questions.question: In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. An optimal assignment of cost $z$ is known. One pair is then forbidden and the problem is solved again with optimal cost $z'$, assuming an allowed complete assignment still exists. Which relation must hold?
options: $z'\le z$, because a ban removes a costly option
$z'\ge z$, because fewer assignments are allowed
$z'>z$, because the ban always destroys the optimum
$z'=z$, because only one pair of $n^2$ is removed

questions.question: In an assignment problem, $n$ agents each receive exactly one of $n$ tasks and each task goes to exactly one agent, with cost $c_{ij}$ for agent $i$ doing task $j$. A forbidden pair is modelled by a finite penalty $M$ instead of $\infty$, but in fact no complete assignment avoids all forbidden pairs. What happens when the model is solved?
options: It returns an assignment through a penalty $M$, at a finite cost.
It reports that no assignment exists, as with $\infty$ entries.
It returns the best allowed assignment after removing $M$ again.
It fails only when $M$ is smaller than all ordinary costs.

questions.question: Three agents (rows) and three tasks (columns) have costs $\begin{pmatrix}2&4&6\\5&3&4\\7&6&2\end{pmatrix}$, and each agent gets exactly one task and each task one agent. Without restrictions the diagonal, cost 7, is optimal. Agent 2 is then forbidden from task 2. What is the new minimum total cost?

Three agents (rows) and three tasks (columns) have costs $\begin{pmatrix}2&6&7\\5&3&8\\4&9&1\end{pmatrix}$, one task per agent and one agent per task. Agent 1 is forbidden from task 1, and the modeller replaces $c_{11}$ by a finite penalty $M$. For which $M$ does every optimal assignment avoid the pair $(1,1)$?
options: Exactly for $M>9$
Exactly for $M>8$
Exactly for $M>12$
Exactly for $M>2$

questions.question: Three agents (rows) and three tasks (columns) have costs $\begin{pmatrix}4&9&3\\6&8&2\\1&8&5\end{pmatrix}$, one task per agent and one agent per task. The minimum cost 12 is reached by $1\to2,2\to3,3\to1$. Agent 1 is then forbidden from task 2. What happens to the minimum total cost?
options: It falls below 12, as the cost 9 is avoided.
It rises to 14, the next best total.
It stays 12, as agent 1 can take task 3 instead.
It becomes infinite, as an optimal pair is banned.

questions.question: In an $n\times n$ assignment problem (one task per agent, one agent per task) all costs are nonnegative, some pairs are forbidden, and one allowed complete assignment of total cost $T$ is known. Every forbidden cost is replaced by the same finite penalty $M$. How does the condition $M>T$ relate to the guarantee that every optimal assignment avoids forbidden pairs?
options: It is required, since any $M\le T$ lets a forbidden pair be chosen.
It is a sufficient condition, though a smaller $M$ may also work.
It is useless, since only $M>\max c_{ij}$ guarantees the ban.
It suffices only if reductions are applied to the matrix first.

questions.question: In a $3\times3$ assignment problem with cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\infty&\infty&4\\2&5&1\\3&6&2\end{pmatrix}$ (rows agents, columns tasks, $\infty$ = forbidden), each agent gets one task and each task one agent. What follows from row 1?
options: No allowed assignment exists, since agent 1 has two bans.
Agent 1 can be left out and given a task after the others.
Task 3 should go to agent 2, whose cost 1 is lowest in column 3.
Agent 1 must do task 3, so task 3 is closed to agents 2 and 3.

questions.question: In a $3\times3$ assignment problem with cost matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&\infty&\infty\\4&\infty&\infty\\6&2&3\end{pmatrix}$ (rows agents, columns tasks, $\infty$ = forbidden), each agent gets one task and each task one agent. Every row and every column contains a finite entry. What is true of this instance?
options: No allowed complete assignment exists: agents 1 and 2 both need task 1.
An allowed assignment exists, since each row and column has a finite entry.
An allowed assignment exists, costing 11 as the sum of the row minima.
Feasibility depends on the cost values, so a full solve is needed first.

questions.question: A $3\times3$ assignment problem (rows agents, columns tasks; one task per agent and one agent per task) forbids the pairs $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$ and $(2,2)$, and an allowed complete assignment still exists. Which single additional ban leaves no allowed complete assignment?
options: Forbidding the pair $(2,3)$
Forbidding the pair $(3,1)$
Forbidding the pair $(3,2)$
Forbidding the pair $(3,3)$
